articles.text: The Havens Dads Club hosted its 18th annual Poker Night on Friday, Jan. 9, at Veterans Hall, raising $66,500 for the school. The final hand of the Texas Hold’em tournament was won by Wildwood dad Patrice Fayet, who held a king of hearts and a four of diamonds. Havens mom Julie Moravy finished in second place. All proceeds from the event went directly to the school, surpassing last year’s total by $4,000. About 130 players took part in the tournament, with an additional 20 attendees purchasing social-only tickets. The evening ran from the first card dealt at 6:30 p.m. through the excitement of the final eight-player table. “The team and I try to dial up the fun factor,” said Havens Dads Club President Ted Kinch. “People can give money because charity demands it or because the school needs funding — or they can play some poker.” Poker Night organizing committee members included Andrew Johnson, Andy Meakins, Babak Sanii, Brandon Bercovich, Kyle Killian, Mike Cvet, and Kinch. This year, the team introduced a perpetual trophy engraved with the names of past winners, with space to add future champions in the years ahead. Players and guests enjoyed food from Robert Dorsey Catering, Arthur Mac Pizza, and Top Dog, along with a full bar. New Photo by Babak Sanii Patice Fayet, winner of the 2026 Havens Poker Tournament.

articles.text: The California Public Utilities Commission has published the Final Environmental Impact Report for Pacific Gas and Electric Company’s Moraga-Oakland X 115-kilovolt Rebuild Project. The Final Environmental Impact Report evaluates potentially significant environmental impacts associated with the project and identifies mitigation measures and alternatives that would avoid or reduce those impacts. After the release of the Final Environmental Impact Report, a CPUC administrative law judge will prepare a proposed decision and present the project to the commission. Commissioners will then consider whether to certify the Environmental Impact Report as meeting the requirements of the California Environmental Quality Act and whether to grant PG&E a Permit to Construct. No construction timeline has been set, and work cannot begin until the CPUC completes this process. The Moraga-Oakland X project proposes upgrades to approximately five miles of four existing 115-kilovolt transmission lines between the Moraga and Oakland X substations. The route passes through the City of Orinda, unincorporated areas of Contra Costa County, the cities of Oakland and Piedmont, and existing PG&E utility rights-of-way. Within Piedmont, the project would remain within an existing PG&E transmission corridor. Any work in the city would occur along current rights-of-way rather than new routes. The project would rebuild the four overhead transmission lines into four hybrid lines, with approximately four miles remaining overhead and about one mile placed underground. Existing towers, poles, and conductors would be replaced with either overhead or underground components, and minor modifications would be made at existing substations. The rebuild would also include the installation of optical ground wire on aboveground structures, with a communications cable continuing through the underground segments. The Final Environmental Impact Report and related documents are available on the CPUC project website at https://bit. ly/49IGwZB.
articles.title: Final EIR for PG&E’s Moraga-Oakland X 115 kV Rebuild Project

articles.text: City Council will consider adopting a resolution in compliance with California’s Surplus Land Act at its meeting on Tuesday, Jan. 20. Approval would allow the city to take the next step toward implementing the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Before a city can lease or sell public property, it must follow the requirements of the Surplus Land Act. Recent amendments to the law are intended to promote affordable housing development on surplus public land statewide as a response to California’s housing shortage. The act provides two possible pathways for disposing of land: an “exempt” or a “non-exempt” declaration. Planning and Building Director Kevin Jackson outlined the differences between the two approaches in a press release issued earlier this week. For non-exempt sites, the state sets the process for notifying developers, establishes negotiation parameters and determines which developers receive preference, leaving the city with limited control. For exempt sites, the city has greater flexibility to select a developer based on local criteria, but the pathway comes with deeper Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson on the video discussing the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan affordable housing requirements. In practice, this generally means a higher share of units must be reserved for lower-income households and remain affordable for longer periods than under the standard non-exempt process. Jackson wrote that the exempt option aligns with the goals of the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. “These deeper affordability requirements associated with an ‘exempt’ determination are consistent with the affordable housing targets that already exist in the adopted Specific Plan,” Jackson said. In December, the California Department of Housing and Community Development confirmed that a Moraga Canyon project would qualify for an exempt determination. City Council is now considering a resolution to pursue that path in order to retain greater local control. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan remains controversial among some residents living along Moraga Avenue. Several households have posted signs expressing concern about traffic and safety, particularly for children biking along the roadway. In response, the city has released an informational video addressing these concerns, available on the City of Piedmont’s YouTube channel at https://bit. ly/4r5vHYP The sign showing displeasure with the housing plan, placed in front of a house on Moraga Avenue Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Record breaking dollar amounts and participation Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has announced that this year’s Giving Campaign has raised more than $4,000,000 in gifts and pledges in support of Piedmont’s public schools. This represents an increase of 9% over last year and is the strongest Giving Campaign in history. Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn have led the Giving Campaign for the past three years, raising increasing amounts each year, totalling over $11,000,000 for Piedmont’s public schools. When asked about their success, Osborn shared, “Our community gets it. We’ve all seen the increasing costs of living and doing business, and the increasing needs of our schools. We know what we want for our kids and our community is here to meet those needs.” Hunter added, “It seems to me that the community made a really loud statement this year about what is important. The Giving Campaign exists to continue the betterment of our public schools, and that’s something we have control over. Our community has been showing up for our schools for 50 years and we’ll keep showing up for 50 more.” So far this year, PEF has received gifts and pledges from 1,161 households, the highest number of donor households since 2022. Parent participation is currently at 61%; the final total will be calculated at the end of June as donors will have until then to make their Giving Campaign contribution for the year. The Giving Campaign would like to congratulate the 1st grade families for winning the class participation challenge with 79% overall participation. 3rd grade families came in second place with 74%. Across schools, Beach has the highest participation at 76% followed by Havens at 73%, Wildwood at 68%, PMS at 58% and PHS/MHS at 50%. Approximately $300,000 of Giving Campaign contributions are donor designated to the endowment fund. At the end of the school year, PEF will add the remaining $3.7 million to the endowment distribution and other fundraisers, subtract expenses, and grant those funds to PUSD for the 2026-27 academic year. A survey will be released this spring to ascertain parent funding priorities for the grant. PEF thanks everyone that made a contribution, reached out to their company as part of the corporate matching program, contributed via DAF, and talked to neighbors and friends about the importance of The Giving Campaign. Every single donation, no matter the amount, supports the students and the schools. Catie Osborn (left) and Kim Hunter, chairs of the 2025-26 Giving Campaign, celebrate surpassing $4 million for Piedmont schools.

articles.text: The stars in our sky are among the greatest things humans share. No matter where we are in the world, the same stars stretch above our heads. Every day, stars are born and, like humans, they Stars form inside nebulae, vast molecular clouds made of gas and dust. These star-forming regions, often called stellar nurseries, contain all the building blocks Stellar nursery nebulae are rich in hydrogen and helium, the primary gases involved in star formation. In the cold temperatures of a nebula, gases clump together, creating regions of higher density. Over time, these regions collect more matter, increasing their mass and strengthening their gravitational pull. As gravity causes the material to collapse inward, friction generates heat. Eventually, this process ignites, and a star is born. While some nebulae mark the beginning of a star’s life, others form after a star’s death. What happens at the end of a star’s life depends largely on its mass. When a low-mass star dies, it sheds its outer layers, creating an expanding cloud of gas and dust known as a planetary nebula. When a high-mass star reaches the end of its life, it explodes in a powerful event called a supernova. In the aftermath, the remaining material spreads into space and can eventually become part of new nebulae, supplying the raw ingredients for future stars. A nebula near you Not every nebula is visible from Earth, but some can be seen with the naked eye under the right conditions. In the Northern Hemisphere at this time of year, the Orion Nebula, also known as Messier 42, is one of the most famous examples. Located about 1,500 light-years away, it is the closest stellar nursery to Earth. With a telescope, its structure and activity become even more striking, offering observers a rare glimpse into the process of star formation. The stars are closer than you think The Chabot Space & Science Center offers free public telescope viewings every Friday and Saturday from 7:30 to 10:30 p.m., weather permitting. During these sessions, visitors can learn about the center’s historic telescopes and observe stars, planets and other celestial objects. For those interested in an even closer look at the cosmos, Chabot also hosts small astrophotography workshops. Participants learn how to operate telescope rigs and create polished night-sky photographs of their own. The next astrophotography class is scheduled for Jan. 29, offering an out-of-thisworld opportunity to explore the universe through the lens. You can find more information about these programs and more at chabotspace.org. The magic of the Milky Way is closer than you think

Over time, these regions collect more matter, increasing their mass and strengthening their gravitational pull. As gravity causes the material to collapse inward, friction generates heat. Eventually, this process ignites, and a star is born. While some nebulae mark the beginning of a star’s life, others form after a star’s death. What happens at the end of a star’s life depends largely on its mass. When a low-mass star dies, it sheds its outer layers, creating an expanding cloud of gas and dust known as a planetary nebula. When a high-mass star reaches the end of its life, it explodes in a powerful event called a supernova. In the aftermath, the remaining material spreads into space and can eventually become part of new nebulae, supplying the raw ingredients for future stars. A nebula near you Not every nebula is visible from Earth, but some can be seen with the naked eye under the right conditions. In the Northern Hemisphere at this time of year, the Orion Nebula, also known as Messier 42, is one of the most famous examples. Located about 1,500 light-years away, it is the closest stellar nursery to Earth. With a telescope, its structure and activity become even more striking, offering observers a rare glimpse into the process of star formation. The stars are closer than you think The Chabot Space & Science Center offers free public telescope viewings every Friday and Saturday from 7:30 to 10:30 p.m., weather permitting. During these sessions, visitors can learn about the center’s historic telescopes and observe stars, planets and other celestial objects. For those interested in an even closer look at the cosmos, Chabot also hosts small astrophotography workshops. Participants learn how to operate telescope rigs and create polished night-sky photographs of their own. The next astrophotography class is scheduled for Jan. 29, offering an out-of-thisworld opportunity to explore the universe through the lens. You can find more information about these programs and more at chabotspace.org. articles.text: (Beach 5th grader) You think math is boring? Think again! More than 120 Piedmont kids and adults came together last Wednesday, January 14 at Ellen Driscoll to celebrate math. No matter what game you were playing, there was fun to be had at the Advancing Learning for Piedmont Students (ALPS) Math Fair. Games like Prime Climb were big hits, and roulette and bingo attracted large crowds. The most surprising part was that chess was the most popular game, with spectators gathering around to watch. “All 11 games were a hit, but chess was the most popular,” said volunteer Ariel Shusteff. There were games for everyone, from first grade all the way to tenth grade. Another great thing about the event was seeing older kids teaching younger kids how to play the math games. The camaraderie created a really nice overall vibe for all. “I loved how many games there were. I had so much fun with my friends,” said Rydia Sun. But the whole point of the math event was “to bring people together and have fun while learning math,” said Ella Grossberg, an ALPS member and the event organizer. And it wasn’t just math. You could earn candy for playing games, and there was even a snack bar just outside. Many Piedmont community members also came out to show support. School board member Susy Struble and Board VP Michael Malione discussed an interesting book brought by Maxim Shusteff about using technology in the classroom. Superintendent Dr. Hawn and Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich checked out the Math Kangaroo competition information table too. One of the best parts was when Kate Waldron, a teacher and head of the math department, brought super challenging practice questions for the AMC 8 competition. It took three kids and 30 minutes to finally solve one really hard problem, but they did it! “So much fun and so many games!” said Luke Shin about the Math Fair. Linda Tao, one of the organizers, wondered if it would make sense to have this event more than once a year. With candy prizes and an insane amount of pizza, this kid’s vote is a big YES. articles.text: Piedmont’s 29th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 19 included a display in the Alan Harvey Theater of Piedmont student artwork and literature. More than 130 students submitted artwork or writing pieces, showcasing the next generation’s creative representations on Dr. King’s legacy. The theme guiding the art was: “In his 1967 book, Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. asked, ‘Where Do We Go from Here? Chaos or Community?’ What do you choose? What would you like our future to look like?” This was the fifth year that Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) has hosted the student showcase. Most of the student submissions came from Havens and Wildwood students, and one PHS student, Hunter Fasteau, the school’s fall representative to the school board. Most of the work came from 3rd, 4th and 5th graders whom were instructed to create 2-D art, photos, essays, or poems in response to the theme. Some teachers had their students create the art as a class or talked about the theme and the showcase in class. PADC President Ellen Lee was thankful for the large student response this year. w ww ww w. .w wi il ld dw wo oo od dc cr ra ab bf fe ee ed d. .c co om m

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team split its last two games against Western Alameda County Conference opponents, falling 2-0 to Castro Valley on Tuesday, January 13 at the Trojans’ field, and winning 4-0 over Alameda at Witter Field on Friday, January 16. It was a stellar performance by senior Arden Sorensen-Wald against Alameda, scoring two goals and an assist. Both of her goals came from distance, including a free kick from 34 yards out and another shot from 29 yards in open play. “We noticed that their goalie was a little shorter, so we wanted to shoot it over her. The second goal was a whole team effort. We were passing around and I got it to around the top of the box where I could get a nice strike on it,” Sorensen-Wald said. Against the Hornets, the Highlanders posed a lot of problems with an aggressive press and frequently looked to get the ball up the field. Piedmont’s last goal was an example. Sorensen-Wald played a long pass to Miranda Liu who sprinted by Alameda’s back line to land her second goal of the game. “We are super direct and just constantly getting forward. Miranda is key to that; it wouldn’t work without her,” SorensenWald said. 4-0 over Alameda Piedmont’s first goal came in the 18th minute when SorensenWald launched her long free kick from 34 yards, placing it above the keeper. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team lost a pair of games on the road last week, falling 1-0 to Berkeley on Friday, January 16 and 2-1 at Mt. Eden in Hayward on Wednesday, January 14. The Highlanders are struggling to create offensive opportunities on consistent occasion after losing most of its roster from last year’s team. With a young group, coach Ben Russell knew there would be an adjustment period. “We talk about being a taxi driver as opposed to being a bus driver. A bus driver has the same loop over and over, a taxi driver goes to multiple destinations. We need to solve multiple problems and understand there are multiple ways to play the game. The ability to solve multiple problems is what we are lacking right now,” Russell said. 1-0 loss to Berkeley The Yellowjackets had many shot attempts in the first 40 minutes, but only two were on target and were easily handled by goalkeeper Tobias Tsai. In at goalkeeper in the second half Colt Hitchcock, made a big stop in the 47th minute by rushing off his line to thwart a Berkeley forward before he could take a shot. However, Berkeley broke the deadlock in the 51st minute after their right winger wheeled into the area down by the end line, centering a pass while Hitchcock tried to press him. With an empty net, Berkeley scored what proved to be the game-winner. Travers Kemp logged Piedmont’s first shot attempt in the 57th minute when Elias Reed-Miguel sent a long pass toward him when making a run into the box. Kemp leaped to get his head on the ball, but it looped far wide of the mark. Shortly after, Kemp nearly scored in the 60th minute when splitting two defenders with a nifty touch, taking a low rolling shot from atop the box that forced a diving save out of Berkeley’s keeper. 2-1 loss to Mt. Eden Piedmont scored the game’s first goal in the 15th minute. After a corner sailed through the area to the right side, Maxwell Rodriguez gained possession near the right corner flag, turning to send a cross on his first touch. His pass took one bounce, finding Reed-Miguel standing unmarked. Reed-Miguel caught it out of the air and sent a header into the net. Six minutes later, Tsai made a huge diving save to keep PHS ahead. Mt. Eden found the equalizer Staff Photos Elias Reed-Miguel scored Piedmont’s only goal against Mt. Eden. Travers Kemp had a couple of scoring chances against Berkeley. Jackson Van-Kleeck looks to make a play. on a questionable offside no-call. The ball whipped in from the right side found their striker in close distance in front of the net. The Monarchs’ forward looked a couple of feet past Piedmont’s back line when the ball was played. The Monarchs’ game-winner came in the 71st. This time, a low pass was played down the right wing. Hitchcock rushed off his line to greet the attacker at the top of the area, but the Mt. Eden forward took a nice touch past the keeper and slotted the ball into the empty net. articles.text: [Reprinted from January 2021] We return to one of our earlier Hiking With Jon ventures from 2021, where you can find groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees in Portola State Park. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within Portola Redwoods. Aside from the awe striking size, the thousand year old tree is among the few old growths to make it through the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill ascent through the hill sides for near two-miles and gaining 550 feet in elevation until intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail—turning left to start your loop back to your car, intersecting with Peter’s Creek. Turning right starts a 1.5 mile hike to a historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and jolting 500 feet in elevation until its end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than 6-feet wide, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. If you turned left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until intersecting with a T—turning right to make our way to Upper Escape Road, turning right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car—making it a 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. But it’s worth noting that Downed trees line your path on many of the 18 miles of hiking trails at Portola Redwoods State Park. Take the Summit Trail to start your loop. The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail.

articles.text: Light festival ends Jan. 25 Oakland Zoo’s popular “Glowfari” evening light festival ends on January 25. Glowfari features hundreds of life-sized glowing animal lanterns and all-new light fixtures this year. The family-friendly lantern festival invites guests to stroll among larger-than-life illuminated animal sculptures during festival hours from 4:30 to 9 p.m. “Glowfari” joins dozens of holiday-themed light festivals across the Bay Area, but this long standing event, previously named “Zoolights,” focuses on wildlife, sustainability and animal conservation. The reinvented event features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates and has been a wildly successful fundraiser for the Zoo since its inception. Each handcrafted lantern creates a colorful journey through Oakland Zoo’s themed zones, including the savanna, the ocean, and a whimsical bug tunnel. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase. While animal displays are closed for late night events, “Glowfari” ticketholders can still take a gondola ride to the California Trail for panoramic views of the illuminated exhibits spread across the zoo’s hillsides. Timed-entry tickets are required and often sell out early. Admission prices vary by date, and parking is included with each reservation. Children under two are free. Proceeds from Glowfari help support the Oakland Zoo’s wildlife conservation programs and animal care initiatives. More information is available at www.oaklandzoo.org. Tickets are available online for Oakland Zoo’s annual light festival.

articles.text: Museum offers football-themed programs, workshops first week of February The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is inviting the public to experience this year’s Super Bowl through art by offering a variety of public art displays, workshops and programs leading up to the event. SFMOMA will unveil the official Super Bowl XL roman numerals in its Evelyn and Walter Haas Jr. Atrium on January 29. The addition will be on view through February 8, offering a free public viewing ahead of the Super Bowl in the Bay Area. The installation is part of a broader partnership between SFMOMA and the Bay Area Host Committee surrounding Super Bowl LX. The museum will also host several public programs and events during the first week of February. On Thursday, February 5, SFMOMA and the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) will present “Building Universes,” an evening program running from 5 to 8 p.m. The event will feature poetry and dance performances across both institutions, with artists responding to works on view in the galleries. The program is inspired in part by the 1972 Black Art Expo curated by Suzanne Jackson. Photo courtesy of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art SFMOMA will unveil the official Super Bowl XL roman numerals in its Evelyn and Walter Haas Jr. Atrium on January 29. SFMOMA will be closed to the public on Friday, February 6, for the Bay Area Host Committee’s Super Bowl LX Innovation Summit. The invitation-only event is expected to draw about 500 participants from the technology, sports, investment, and cultural sectors. The summit will include main stage sessions and breakout panels focused on technology and innovation in sports and large-scale events. A public workshop on Bay Area graffiti and street art is scheduled for Saturday, February 7, from 2 to 4 p.m. Led by artist and educator Dregs One, the program will explore the history and styles of regional graffiti and include a hands-on component. Artist Ruby Neri will join the discussion during the latter portion of the workshop. Family programming will conclude Sunday, February 8, with a free Family Studio activity from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on the museum’s second floor, where participants can create sportsthemed pennants. The museum store will also offer limited-edition hats throughout February while supplies last. For more information on Super Bowl-themed programming at SFMOMA, visit www. SFMOMA.org.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco is showing Tennessee Williams’s landmark play A Streetcar Named Desire at the historic Toni Rembe Theater from January 21 to February 1. Streetcar is a classic 1947 play following Southern belle Blanche DuBois, who moves in with her sister Stella and brutish brotherin-law Stanley Kowalski in New Orleans, leading to a clash of cultures, desires, and illusions that ends in tragedy. A.C.T. ‘s production features intimate staging and seating in the round by utilizing onstage seats. Director Nick Westrate presents Williams’s complete, unabridged text with four performers and no props. The cast includes Screen Actors Guild and Theater World Award-winner Heather Lind, as well as Brad Koed, James Russell, and Lucy Owen, under the direction of Nick Westrate. “After touring A Streetcar Named Desire to found spaces around the country for three years, we can’t believe we are finally bringing it…to a theater,” said co-creators Lucy Owen and Westrate. “We are thrilled to be collaborating with Pam MacKinnon and all of the amazing artists at A.C.T. to explore what it means to use a theater as a found space. We can’t wait to let Tennessee Williams’s beautiful souls haunt San Francisco.” A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon said she “leapt at the chance to make A.C.T. ‘s Toni Rembe Theater a found space for this acting troupe to storm and haunt.” “I saw this production from The Streetcar Project in a Brooklyn warehouse in 2024. The performances were harrowingly lived in. This canonical American play delivered simply, lovingly, anew,” MacKinnon said in a press release. Single tickets (ranging from $25–$130) are on sale now at the A.C.T. Box Office at 415-749-2228 or online at act-sf.org/streetcar. articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato Cal Performances at UC Berkeley will present mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato with the genre-crossing string trio Time for Three in Emily – No Prisoner Be, a new, evening-length song cycle by Pulitzer Prize–winning composer Kevin Puts, on Saturday, February 7 at 8 p.m. in Zellerbach Hall. The new work sets 24 poems by Emily Dickinson to composer Kevin Puts’ score, featuring stage lighting design from Andrew Staples that the creators say “magnifies the emotional terrain of Dickinson’s language.” Mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato, making her return to the Bay Area following acclaimed projects including Eden (2023) and In War & Peace: Harmony Through Music (2016), leads the program vocally. Each member of Time for Three, including Nicolas Kendall (viola, violin), Charles Yang (violin) and Ranaan Meyer (bass), will perform alongside DiDonato. Time for Three won a Grammy in 2023 for their recording of Puts’s triple concerto Contact. Emily – No Prisoner Be marks DiDonato’s first appearance with Cal Performances in this collaboration and continues her long creative partnership with Puts.She previously performed a lead role in his opera The Hours. A studio recording of Emily – No Prisoner Be is scheduled Composer Kevin Puts for release on January 30, with four tracks already available on streaming platforms: “Because I could not stop for Death —,” “There is another sky,” “Her Face,” and “They shut me up.” The project reflects DiDonato’s advocacy for making music broadly accessible. A throughline of her career alongside accolades including multiple Grammy Awards and the 2018 Olivier Award for Outstanding Achievement in Opera. articles.text: Music and sports share many similarities. Success is measured by a high batting average and errors must be kept to a minimum. The seasons of play are grueling. It is a given that sports heroes must maintain a high level of physical fitness. The same is true with concert musicians. In the past, classical music stars were at the top of the entertainment pay scale. But… things change. Just the other day I noticed that a baseball player signed a contract. The amount was unbelievable… $240 million for four years. Imagine if Babe Ruth or Willie Mays were playing today. If a mediocre, but highly touted, player gets $60 million per year how much would the greatest players of all time get? It’s only January, but I suggest that we begin looking into the future. The concert season used to be from September until the end of May or June. The summers were always reserved for relaxation and study. In Europe, there were absolutely no concerts during the summer. Then the United States initiated music festivals. This idea caught on big time and now the summer season is as busy as the rest of the year. No matter where you go in the world there are music festivals. When I was a kid, the Hollywood Bowl was just about the only summer music festival in Southern California. In Northern California it was the Bach Festival in Carmel. The plot is set in motion by a birthday gift left to Ian by his deceased father: a wizard’s staff, a rare phoenix gem, and instructions for a spell that would allow their father to return for just one day. Ian’s first attempt, with Barley’s encouragement, goes awry, producing only the lower half of their dad — pants, socks and shoes included. To complete the spell, the brothers must find a replacement gemstone, which Barley is convinced he knows how to track down. What follows is a quest movie in classic Pixar form. The brothers set off in Barley’s battered van, bickering over directions and debating Ian’s uneven magical abilities. articles.text: As we drove up the driveway approaching DeLoach Winery I felt I was returning home. That’s because the first wine I fell in love with back in the late 70’s was DeLoach White Zinfandel. This is embarrassing for a wine writer to admit. It was 5 bucks a bottle and I thought it was the most delicious thing I had ever tasted. Here I am 45 years later returning for a taste only to find things had totally changed – for the better. They no longer make White Zinfandel but instead craft an amazing variety of cool climate grapes like Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. DeLoach Vineyards stands as one of the foundational wineries of California’s Russian River Valley, shaping the region’s reputation for world-class Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Zinfandel. Founded in 1975 by Cecil and Christine DeLoach along with partners, the winery grew from a modest estate into a pioneering force in Sonoma County viticulture. Early on, Cecil DeLoach planted some of the valley’s first modern Pinot Noir on the Olivet Bench, recognizing the cooler climate’s affinity with Burgundian varietals, and in 1983 he was among the first producers to use the “Russian River Valley” appellation on a wine label—helping define the region’s identity. Despite rapid growth, financial strains led DeLoach Vineyards into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2003, opening the door for new stewardship. That same year, the winery was purchased by Boisset Family Estates, a Franco-American wine group led by JeanCharles Boisset with deep roots in Burgundy and a commitment to terroir-driven, sustainable winemaking. Under Boisset’s ownership, DeLoach underwent a transformation focused on organic and biodynamic farming. The estate vineyards were replanted with cover crops to restore soil vitality, and in 2008 the property earned organic certification from the California Certified Organic Farmers (CCOF). articles.text: Last Wednesday dawned sunny and mild, and 49 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group, joined by five canine companions, gathered at the Exedra to enjoy it. The pleasant weather made for an inviting start, though the turnout was a little surprising. Walkers had been warned in advance that this would not be an easy route. The group keeps a soft goal of covering every safe walking street in Piedmont each year, but a few had gone untouched in 2025. Those streets tend to sit on the city’s edges and often come with significant elevation. Crest and Somerset roads, branching off Hampton Road, fit that description perfectly. Long, steep, and far from the center of town, they are seldom visited. In fact, the group had walked them only twice in its eight-year history. With the weather cooperating, it seemed like a good morning to take on the challenge. Adding another dimension to the outing, walker and Piedmont historian Meghan Bennett provided historical context on the early St. James Wood real estate development, making the walk as much about learning as exercise. From the Exedra, the group made its way up Highland, Sheridan, Wildwood and Crocker avenues, reaching Hampton Road in a long line before regrouping at Hampton Park. There, Bennett shared the story of St. James Wood. The land in eastern Piedmont was originally owned by Frank C. Havens and F. M. “Borax” Smith’s Realty Syndicate, formed in 1895. The two men had begun acquiring large tracts of East Bay land even earlier, with Smith buying streetcar lines in 1890 as the backbone of what became the Key System transit empire. Altogether, they assembled roughly 20 square miles of land across Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley and developed notable landmarks, including the Claremont Hotel. Havens, however, ran into serious financial trouble in the mid-1910s and sold off nearly all of his land and other assets before his death in 1918. In the 1920s, the St. James Wood property was acquired by James Howard L’Hommedieu, born in New York in 1884 and later a resident of Oakland and Piedmont. L’Hommedieu saw the site as an opportunity to create something finer in residential development than had ever been attempted in the East Bay. He believed Piedmont was restricted to homes of “the better type” and that eastern, or “upper,” Piedmont had already established itself as “the site of the finest homes in the bay district.” In his view, this “high-class district” needed room to expand, and St. James Wood was the only place it could. L’Hommedieu laid out a subdivision of winding streets and spacious homesites. All utility wires were placed underground, and he spent thousands of dollars on trees, shrubs and lawns. Six entrances to the development featured “stately gates” formed by pairs of white columns. Parks were included, and each section of sidewalk throughout the neighborhood was marked with four terracotta tiles set into the concrete. It was the Roaring Twenties, and money did not appear to be a limiting factor. He also established strict development restrictions to ensure each home fit its surroundings. Minimum construction costs ranged from $6,000 to $15,000 depending on location, and designs had to be approved by a board of leading architects. These guarantees were to be maintained under a plan overseen by the St. James Wood Homes Association, founded in 1926 to govern the neighborhood. Construction began that year and continued through the mid-1960s. In a testament to the area’s enduring appeal, a home on one of the last remaining, very steep lots on St. James Drive was built as recently as 2018. Many of the neighborhood’s homes were designed by individual builders working alongside prominent architects. L’Hommedieu died in 1950 at age 66 and is buried in Mountain View Cemetery. At its height, the St. James Wood Homes Association represented more than 185 homes. Its covenants, conditions and restrictions required board approval for changes to exterior color schemes and for tree removals. Owners also needed approval for changes to the location or height of structures, including walls and fences. Annual dues were $25. The last annual meeting was held in 2012. Phil Chin, a neighborhood resident, said he received notice a few years ago that the association was being dissolved and that the roughly $1,000 remaining in its bank account was donated to charity. After a group photo at Hampton Park, some walkers opted for a shorter route and returned toward the city center. The rest crossed La Salle Avenue and passed through the large white columns flanking Hampton Road that mark the main entrance to St. James Wood. Piedmont can require you to clean up vegetation and add defensible space, and if you ignore notices, the City can do the work, bill you, and lien your property. In the Other News As of January 1, 2026, California’s new habitability law (AB 628) quietly raises the bar for every landlord in the state: working stoves and refrigerators are now legally part of “basic” habitability, right alongside heat and hot water. In plain English, landlords must provide and maintain a stove that safely cooks food and a refrigerator that safely stores it in order to legally collect rent. This seems like common sense until you think about the hotplates (dating myself) and microwave kitchenettes that seem so common in yesteryear’s college towns. Reader Question This week’s reader question brings to mind one of FDR’s classic bon mots: “There is nothing I love as much as a good fight.” –Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Interview, N.Y. Times, 22 Jan. 1911 Q: My neighbor’s fence is falling into our yard and a couple of their trees are coming over to our side of the property line. They’ve been promising to “do something about it” for a few years now, but nothing ever happens. What can I do beside keep asking them to do something? A: If your neighbor keeps promising to fix the fence or trim their trees and nothing happens, stop waiting and start acting. In California you can trim branches back to the property line and you can always send written notice and involve the city if needed. But before you escalate, be honest about whether the problem is really worth the time, attorneys, and aggravation—it’s usually cheaper to handle repairs yourself, ideally with your neighbor’s cooperation. The smartest move is a calm heads‑up. Let them know you’re planning to shore up the fence and trim the trees at your expense and ask them to work with you; it typically saves money, time, and, quite literally, mends fences. Did You Know We all know where Mulberry’s Market is, but Piedmont’s first “Mulberry business” wasn’t selling coffee and sandwiches—it was raising silkworms. In 1885, the Ladies Silk Culture Society launched Piedmont’s first real “industry”. A 15‑acre silk farm planted in mulberries near what are now Dudley Avenue and Littlewood Drive, where young women lived on site, tended silkworms, and reeled cocoons in a two‑story workhouse overlooking open country. It was a bold attempt to create respectable, self‑supporting work for women, but local labor costs couldn’t compete with cheap imported silk from China, and the operation shut down after roughly ten years. articles.text: Pictured inside the entrance to the Buck Institute for Research on Aging are docent Mike Noel (left), Jim Ayotte, Janice Subotnick, Elene Manolis, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Judy Wang, Edith Hereso, Yorkman Lowe, Sue Getreuer, Sandra Ponce, Carole Jones, Gloria Wilmer, Greg Jurin, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Susan Silva, and George Epstein. The Piedmont Seniors recently traveled to Novato for a guided tour of the Buck Institute, a research center focused exclusively on the biology of aging. Its work aims to help people live not only longer lives, but healthier ones. Research has shown that aging is the No. 1 risk factor for chronic disease, and the Buck’s mission is to end the threat of age-related disease for this and future generations. The institute’s vision is that people should be able to enjoy life at 95 as much as they do at 25, a goal that requires a deeper understanding of how aging itself works. As the world’s first independent biomedical research institute, the Buck had a running start in the field. It is home to the nation’s first PhD program in the biology of aging. What once sounded like science fiction is now established fact: aging is malleable. Discoveries at the Buck are already being translated into drug-based and lifestyle interventions designed to help people live better, longer lives. The institute’s goal is to develop new therapies and interventions that improve what researchers call “healthspan.” The Buck Institute employs 270 people, including 170 scientists, representing 37 different countries. According to Eric Verdin, The buck Institute docent, Mike Noel, is showing the Piedmont Seniors a miniature scale of the Buck campus. MD, the Buck Institute’s president and CEO, “What I want people to know about the Buck is the incredible commitment and excitement that permeates the walls of this institution. We are pushing the frontiers in an area that is going to impact all of humanity. I cannot tell you exactly when this will happen, but I can tell you big discoveries are in the works and will come out of the Buck.” Tours and periodic seminars are open to the public, with seminars and Zoom meetings available for a nominal fee. After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors took a short drive around the area before heading to HopMonk Tavern in Novato for lunch. HopMonk is a casual restaurant known for its inviting beer garden, varied menu and friendly service. Overall, it was a wonderful and enlightening day for everyone. articles.text: Winter in Piedmont brings cooler temperatures, seasonal rain, and a natural slowdown in outdoor activity. While February may feel like a quieter time of year, it is actually one of the most important months for homeowners to assess, protect, and maintain their homes. Thoughtful winter care not only preserves a property’s condition but also prevents small issues from becoming costly repairs. Inspect Roofs, Gutters, and Drainage: Piedmont homes, many of them older and architecturally distinctive, are especially vulnerable to winter wear. Rain highlights problem areas that may go unnoticed during dry months. Homeowners should check roofs for loose tiles, worn flashing, or signs of leaks. Gutters and downspouts should be cleared of debris to allow proper water flow and reduce the risk of water pooling near foundations. Ensuring that soil slopes away from the home helps prevent moisture intrusion and long-term structural damage. Heating Systems and Fireplace Safety: have been running for several months. A mid-season check of furnaces or HVAC systems can confirm that everything is operating efficiently and safely. Fireplaces and chimneys should be inspected and cleaned if they’ve been used regularly, as buildup can create fire hazards. Smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms should be tested, and batteries replaced if needed—simple steps that significantly improve household safety. Watch for Moisture and Air Quality Issues: Cool weather combined with rain can create ideal conditions for moisture accumulation. Basements, crawl spaces, garages, and window frames are common areas where condensation or dampness may appear. Homeowners should look for musty odors, peeling paint, or visible mold. Addressing moisture early helps protect indoor air quality and prevents damage to walls, flooring, and insulation. Exterior Maintenance Still Matters: While winter is not typically a time for major landscaping, basic exterior maintenance remains important. Overgrown branches should be trimmed back from roofs and gutters to reduce storm damage risk. Loose fencing, gates, or handrails should be secured, and exterior lighting checked for safety and visibility during shorter days. These small efforts contribute to overall home longevity and neighborhood appeal. Use Winter as a Planning Period: February is also an ideal time to review household paperwork and long-term plans. Organizing insurance policies, warranties, and property records can simplify future decisions. For homeowners considering renovations, downsizing, or a future move, winter provides a calm window to explore options and prepare without pressure. Taking a proactive approach during winter helps Piedmont homeowners maintain their properties, protect their investments, and enter the spring season with confidence and clarity. articles.text: One of the most common concerns among parents of young puppies is car sickness. Many new owners arrive to collect their eight-week-old bundle of joy, only to receive an unwelcome surprise in their lap on the drive home. While most dogs will eventually grow out of car sickness, there are several steps you can take during puppyhood to make travel easier for both you and your dog. So what causes car sickness in puppies? In most cases, it stems from their still-developing inner ears. The vestibular system, which controls balance, is not yet fully mature, leading to sensory confusion between what the puppy sees and what it feels during movement. This mismatch can cause nausea and may be worsened by stress. Common symptoms include excessive drooling, restlessness, frequent yawning, lethargy, shaking or trembling, and, of course, dry heaving and vomiting. There are several simple ways to improve your puppy’s comfort during car rides. Cracking a window can provide fresh air, and allowing your puppy to see outside may help their inner ear better process movement. Puppies who ride in the trunk are far more likely to experience car sickness. An elevated puppy booster seat can also improve visibility and make the ride more comfortable. Your veterinarian may recommend a medication called Cerenia (maropitant citrate) to prevent nausea and vomiting. When given a few hours before travel, it is often very effective, though it can be expensive. Ask your vet about possible over-the-counter alternatives such as meclizine or Dramamine. It is important to remember that dosages for dogs are very different from those for humans, so never give your puppy human medication without Missy the Australian Shepherd enjoying a drive car sicknessfree! veterinary guidance. Even if your puppy gets carsick on every ride, a little planning can go a long way in reducing stress. For longer trips, typically 30 minutes or more, avoid feeding your puppy within two hours of departure. Bring puppy pads, towels and wipes for easy cleanup. A bib can help keep chest fur clean if your puppy drools excessively. Never reprimand your puppy for car sickness, as this can create a negative association with car rides. Finally, resist the urge to feed your puppy immediately after an episode, even if they appear hungry. Most puppies outgrow car sickness within the first six months of life, but that does not make the experience any less challenging in the moment. With patience and preparation, these tips can help make traveling with your new puppy more manageable for everyone involved. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. articles.text: John K. Uilkema died peacefully at home in Piedmont on January 5, 2026 at the age of 90. John was born in Illinois on March 11, 1935 to Mildred and T. John Uilkema. John grew up in Indiana. He attended the University of Michigan, obtaining a degree in Mechanical Engineering. He then studied law at George Washington University in Washington D.C. at night while he worked by day as a patent examiner. Upon graduation from law school, John married Gayle Burns and they moved to California. John became licensed to practice Patent, Trademark and Copyright Law in multiple jurisdictions, and started his practice at Shell Oil in Emeryville before transitioning to the patent, trademark and copyright firm of Naylor and Neil in San Francisco, where he soon became a named partner. The couple moved to Moraga where their daughter Lynn was born. Shortly after, their daughter Sharon was born and the family moved to Lafayette. In the 1980’s, John moved his law practice to Limbach, Limbach and Sutton in the Ferry Building of San Francisco where he served for years as managing partner. John was very active in the American Bar Association and held positions on the Board of Directors. He was president of the Patent Section and was elected to the House of Delegates for multiple decades well past retirement. He received numerous awards for over 50 years of service. Later in his career, he worked at Thelen, Reid and Preist and then at the boutique Intellectual Property firm of Dergosits & Noah. On a personal level, John married the love of his life, Gail Anderson in 1996. They lived in Piedmont with Gail’s son Yung. John was passionate about cars, showing numerous cars over the years including his original 1957 Chevy Bel Air Convertible. He served as a car show judge, and attended the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance annually on Gail’s birthday. His home office was filled with car awards and memorabilia. He was an active member of the Candy Store in Burlingame, where he kept his Chevy on display. John shared his love of cars with his best friend George Marin. The two not only raced, but also enjoyed weekly breakfasts at his favorite place, the Orinda Village Cafe. Throughout his life, John spent much time John Uilkema died peacefully at home in Piedmont on January 5, 2026. exploring his Dutch roots and connecting with his relatives in the Netherlands. John is survived by his wife Gail, daughters Lynn (Damien), Sharon (Curtiss), and grandchildren Natalie, Nicholas, Henry and Sophie. He is predeceased by his younger sister Jackie. To do something in memory of John, please go to the Orinda Village Cafe and have a lovely meal and think of him. He would recommend the three-egg omelet with the waffle.

Finally, resist the urge to feed your puppy immediately after an episode, even if they appear hungry. Most puppies outgrow car sickness within the first six months of life, but that does not make the experience any less challenging in the moment. Homes along Crest span several decades, from the 1920s through the 1950s. Crest begins with a moderate slope, but over roughly a quarter mile the grade increases sharply toward Somerset Road. Walkers paused to admire a home with a dramatic steep slate roof before turning onto Somerset, where the climb remained demanding. Somerset starts very steep and gradually levels out. The hillsides showed signs of past slides, with some homes perched on significant slopes. Farther up stood a large, modern, multi-story white house with a metal gate blocking its steep driveway. Scaffolding surrounded the exterior as it was being painted by a worker clearly untroubled by heights. The house had the feel of a fortress overlooking the valley below. The group crossed the Oakland-Piedmont city line twice and continued for nearly another half mile before emerging on Estates Drive. A lingering haze muted what might otherwise have been expansive views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco. By then the temperature had risen, jackets were shed, and a cool breeze was welcome. The walkers headed down Estates to the top of the steep upper stretch of Hampton Road, descended it, and returned toward town via La Salle Avenue and St. James Drive, noting a set of smaller columns that mark yet another entrance to the St. James Wood neighborhood. At four miles and just under two hours, it was a longer walk than usual. Still, the group took pride in meeting the challenge. It was a satisfying way to begin 2026 for the Walking on Wednesdays group, combining history, scenery and a reminder that some of Piedmont’s most rewarding streets require a bit of extra effort to reach. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to call (510) 420-3070 for more information.
